name: Cerutti Mastodon site
hook: Broken mastodon bones beside heavy cobbles in a San Diego freeway cut, dated to about 130,000 years ago.
claim: Holen and colleagues argued that an unidentified Homo species broke a mastodon's limb bones and molars with stone hammers on stone anvils about 130,000 years ago, for marrow or tool material. That is over 100,000 years before the oldest accepted American sites.

claimed_age.label: ~130,700 ± 9,400 years ago (U-series)
claimed_age.basis: 230Th/U on cortical bone of three mastodon bones, diffusion–adsorption–decay model (USGS); 2σ range. Not radiocarbon; ka taken as calendar years before present.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: People entered the Americas after ~16,000 years ago; the earliest securely dated sites are under ~15,000 years old.

key_critics: Todd J. Braje and nine co-authors

unambiguous_signal.note: Broken bone and battered cobbles only: no knapped tools, cut marks or hominin remains. Natural and machine breakage were argued from the start.

documented_context.note: Grid-mapped excavation with sediment and soil study, but found during freeway construction, which destroyed an unknown, probably significant part of the bonebed.

multiple_dating_methods.note: Only U-series gave ~130 ka. OSL gave 69–99 ka or saturated minimum ages (read as >60–70 ka); radiocarbon failed for lack of collagen.

multiple_labs.note: The ~130 ka bone ages come from one lab (USGS). OSL ran at two other labs; two radiocarbon labs found no collagen.

professional_recovery.note: Excavated over about five months from November 1992 by San Diego Natural History Museum paleontologists.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Full report with extensive supplementary data in Nature, 2017.

material_accessible.note: 3D models and videos were published (Magnani et al. 2019); Gruhn (2018) and Sutton et al. (2019) examined the collection.

independent_teams.note: No independent dating or excavation. Outside researchers made brief re-examinations: Gruhn (2018), supportive on break age; Sutton et al. (2019), critical.

proponent_stake.note: No commercial, religious or nationalist motive documented; the authors declared no competing financial interests.

objections.text: Heavy earth-moving equipment during the freeway work, not people, may have broken the bones.
objections.outcome_note: Proponents and Gruhn (2018), who examined the bones, report old soil carbonate on break surfaces. Haynes (2018) says machine damage is still not ruled out; Ferrell (2019) blames construction.

objections.text: The bones may have broken naturally, for example when other mastodons trampled the carcass, with no human involvement.
objections.outcome_note: Proponents cite low-energy burial, impact notches, cone flakes and refits against natural breakage. No controlled comparison has tested it.

objections.text: Common geological and taphonomic processes explain the site better; the cobbles need not be tools.
objections.outcome_note: Holen et al. (2018) find no trace of the alluvial fan Ferraro et al. propose. Bordes et al. (2020, same team) found bone residue on the worn faces of two cobbles, not their other faces.

objections.text: No knapped stone tools, cut marks or hominin bones were found, so nothing at the site is unambiguously human-made.
objections.outcome_note: Proponents reply that knapped tools are not required at bone-processing sites. No unambiguous artifact is reported in the later work reviewed here.

objections.text: The 230Th/U bone age may be unreliable: bone takes up uranium after burial, and no strictly local uranium source was sampled.
objections.outcome_note: No independent re-dating yet. Proponents cite regular uranium profiles in three bones; OSL gave only >60–70 ka minimums and radiocarbon failed.

objections.text: A 130,000-year-old site implies an unknown hominin in the Americas, with no fossil, archaeological or genomic trace in northeast Asia or the Americas.
objections.raised_by: Todd J. Braje and nine co-authors
objections.outcome_note: Holen et al. (2018) reply that critics misuse 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence'. A prior alone cannot settle the site.

objections.text: The breakage experiments were few, qualitative and uncontrolled, and did not test natural alternatives.
objections.outcome_note: Holen, Fullagar and Holen replied (2019). A 2026 review of 12 proboscidean breakage experiments found most inconsistent and lacking quantitative data.

status_note: Not widely accepted: critics favor natural or construction breakage and doubt the age, while the authors and some supporters (e.g. Gruhn) hold that people broke the bones. No independent re-dating or re-analysis has settled it.

timeline.event: Museum paleontologists monitoring freeway work find the mastodon in November and excavate it over about five months.
Archaeologist Steven Holen first examines the specimens.
A second radiocarbon attempt finds no collagen; OSL work (2008–2011) gives 69–99 ka or saturated minimum ages.
USGS uranium-series work on the bones (2012–2015) yields 130.7 ± 9.4 ka.
Holen et al. publish the claim in Nature.
Critiques by Haynes and by Braje and nine co-authors appear in PaleoAmerica; the authors reply.
Ferraro et al. contest the site in Nature, favoring geological and taphonomic causes; the authors reply.
Gruhn examines the collection and reports soil carbonate on break surfaces, implying ancient breakage.
Ferrell attributes the damage to freeway construction; Sutton et al. favor a natural deposit disturbed by mastodons.
Magnani et al. fault the design of the breakage experiments in an Antiquity debate.
Bordes et al., with two original authors, report bone micro-residue on the worn faces of two cobbles.
Haynes and Krasinski review 12 proboscidean bone-breaking experiments and call for more rigorous design.

decisive_tests.test: Thin-section the carbonate crusts on CM fracture surfaces, and U-series date them where feasible, to see whether the crusts grew over the breaks.
decisive_tests.would_show: Crusts grown over break faces would rule out machine breakage for those bones; fresh breaks cutting through crusts would support it.

decisive_tests.test: Blind, quantitative comparison of CM notches, cone flakes and fracture outlines with controlled sets: hammerstone-on-anvil, trampling, sediment loading and heavy-equipment loading of proboscidean bone.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the CM breakage matches human percussion better than natural or machine breakage.

decisive_tests.test: Repeat the bone U-series at a second laboratory, and date archived Bed E sediment by feldspar post-IR IRSL, which saturates at higher doses than quartz OSL.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the ~130 ka age holds by independent methods, or the bed is younger.

decisive_tests.test: Independent blind use-wear and residue study of all CM cobbles, with control cobbles and sediment from outside the bone clusters.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether bone residue and impact wear are confined to the claimed tool surfaces, as Bordes et al. (2020) report for two cobbles.

falsifier: Refuted if break faces cut through old carbonate crusts, or if controlled natural or machine breakage reproduces the CM notches, cone flakes and cobble wear. Closer to vindicated if independent labs confirm the age and a similar-age site yields unambiguous artifacts.

confidence_note: Supplementary data and Magnani et al. read in full; most critiques and replies read only as abstracts (paywalled). S15 and S19 could not be read.
corrections: Not a skeleton: fragmentary, disarticulated remains of one mastodon. Construction destroyed an unknown, probably significant part of the bonebed before excavation (S2).
Found in November 1992 by museum paleontologists monitoring freeway work and excavated over about five months. The claim was first published in 2017, 24 years later (S18, S1).
The ~130 ka age rests on one method, U-series on bone (130.7 ± 9.4 ka, 2σ). Radiocarbon failed for lack of collagen, and OSL gave only 69–99 ka or saturated minimum ages (S2).
Responses were not all critical: Boëda et al. (2017) and Gruhn (2018) backed the authors, and Gruhn, after examining the bones, rejected the machinery explanation (S13, S10).
Critiques also appeared in Nature (Ferraro et al. 2018) and Antiquity (Magnani et al. 2019), not only in PaleoAmerica.
notes: Named for museum paleontologist Richard Cerutti, who found it. The OSL analyst (S. Forman) later co-authored the Ferraro et al. critique. The authors also suggest a vertically buried tusk may have been placed by people (S2). Haynes et al. 2021 (S15, not read) reportedly show that fracture features thought diagnostic of percussion also arise naturally. independent_methods_count counts bone fractures, cobble wear, refits and clustering, sedimentology and U-series. Even the OSL minimum (>60–70 ka) is far older than accepted sites, so a younger bed would not remove the anomaly.
